item.title: Why Loneliness Programs Are Built for No One
item.description:
Loneliness

Why Loneliness Programs Are Built for No One

Built for an average that doesn't exist, one-size loneliness fixes miss most.

Posted July 9, 2026

Key points
  • The "average" employees well-being programs target don't exist.
  • Social connection spans distinct domains, so people with the same score can be lonely for opposite reasons.
  • In a simulation, matching responses to people's patterns beat one-size and random approaches—at the same cost.
  • The fix isn't more effort from employees; it's an adjustable system that diagnoses before it prescribes.

In the 1950s, the U.S. Air Force had a problem it could not explain. Too many planes were crashing on landing, and not because of the planes. Suspecting the cockpit—designed decades earlier around the dimensions of the "average pilot"—the Air Force measured 4,063 pilots on 10 physical dimensions and asked a simple question: How many fell within the average range on all 10? The answer was zero. The cockpit built for the average fit no one. The eventual fix was not to calculate a better average; it was to make the seat, the pedals, and the straps adjustable.

Most workplace well-being and loneliness programs are that original cockpit. They are built for an average employee—moderately stressed, moderately engaged, probably hybrid—who does not exist.

The Real Costs and Prevalence of Loneliness at Work

This would matter less if connection were a soft perk. It isn't. Loneliness is linked to roughly a 26 percent higher risk of early death; the broader body of social-connection research puts the mortality effect on par with smoking 1-10 cigarettes per day, drawn from data on more than 300,000 people. And it is common at work: in a 2024 Gallup survey, one in five employees said they had felt lonely the previous day; among fully remote workers, it was one in four. And most of them are doing their jobs and sitting in your engagement data with perfectly respectable scores. The biggest lever in your workforce has no sensor.

Why One-Size-Fits-All Interventions Fall Short

Part of why we miss them is that we treat loneliness as a single quantity to be raised or lowered. But social connection is not one thing. In yet unpublished work (preprint of preregistration available here), when our team reviewed how it is actually measured, it split into dozens of distinct domains: how many relationships you have and how often you interact; how close, reciprocal, or conflict-ridden they feel; whether they offer comfort, practical help, or simple recognition; whether you feel appreciated, safe enough to be honest, genuinely heard, or like you belong anywhere at all. Loneliness is what it feels like when one of those threads goes slack—and the slack thread is different from one person to the next. Two employees can post an identical score on a standard screen and be caught in completely different knots: one held in place by insomnia and exhaustion, another by quiet social withdrawal. Hand them the same intervention and, at best, you have helped one of them.

That intuition is testable—though not inside a real organization, since you cannot ethically assign hundreds of people to the wrong help just to see what happens. So we ran it as a simulation. We modeled loneliness not as a single feeling but as a network of interacting components, where a knock to self-worth can deepen a sense of rejection, which in turn makes solitude harder to break. As part of this manuscript, we built three loneliness profiles and ran 2,400 simulated interventions across four strategies: doing nothing; a generic approach that always treated the one symptom most people associate with loneliness; a random approach; and an adaptive one that, for each person, targeted the two components most active and most connected within their particular network.

The crucial detail is what we held constant. Every strategy used the same treatment strength. The only thing that changed was which problem we aimed at, and in whom. That alone produced a clear, reliable advantage: Adaptive targeting beat the generic and random strategies by margins social scientists would call moderate (Cohen's d of 0.45 and 0.39), and beat doing nothing by more still (d = 0.66). In plainer terms, simply aiming the same treatments more precisely produced effects roughly 30 to 230 percent larger than what typical loneliness programs achieve. The more components we could address per person, the wider the gap between smart targeting and guesswork grew.

The Cockpit Lesson for Organizations: Personalization Over Averaging

A simulation is a proof of concept or a promise, and we built in deliberate simplifications. But the logic mirrors the cockpit exactly. The Air Force got nothing from chasing a better average pilot and everything from an adjustable seat. Here, too, the largest untapped gains come not from a better or costlier program, but from fit.

For organizations, that flips the usual script. The dominant model—pick one initiative, roll it out to everyone, count the sign-ups—is the fixed cockpit, the very strategy the simulation beat. When it underperforms, blame tends to slide toward the workforce: they didn't engage, they didn't try. But an engagement survey that flags a "disconnected" team almost never tells you what that disconnection is made of, which is precisely the information a one-size program discards. Personalization, in this light, is not about asking lonely people to work harder on themselves. It is the opposite: It puts the burden on the system to diagnose what each person's disconnection actually is before it prescribes anything.

There is a fair practical question lurking here—whether better fit is worth the effort and cost—and we have begun building tools to estimate it, including a workplace ROI calculator. But that is a story for another post. The deeper point is the one the cockpit taught 70 years ago: The average employee doesn't exist; every actual person in your organization does. Until our programs are built for them rather than for a statistical ghost, we will keep buying cures that, on average, help almost no one. The first move isn't a new program. It's a better question—not How do we get people to connect more, but Whose loneliness is this, and what is it made of?

item.title: What Lies Beneath the Symptoms
item.description:
Mental Health Stigma

What Lies Beneath the Symptoms

Why primary care physicians are already practicing mental healthcare.

Posted July 9, 2026

Key points
  • Primary care physicians now practice at the intersection of medicine and mental health.
  • Integrated health education trains clinicians on the social, emotional, or behavioral factors driving illness.
  • Integrated care allow clinicians to treat not simply the disease, but the person living with it.
  • Understanding a patient's psychology often leads to a better understanding of their physiology.

Mrs. Johnson came to see her primary care physician because her blood pressure was elevated again.

It was the third medication adjustment in less than a year. Her laboratory results were reassuring. She understood the importance of taking her medication, reducing sodium, and exercising regularly. On paper, everything seemed straightforward.

Before ending the visit, her physician asked one more question.

"How have things been at home?"

She paused. Then she began to cry.

Her husband had recently been diagnosed with dementia. She had become his full-time caregiver. She wasn't sleeping. She rarely had time to prepare healthy meals. Exercise had disappeared from her routine. She felt isolated, exhausted, and overwhelmed.

Her hypertension wasn't simply a cardiovascular problem. It was also the physiological expression of chronic psychological stress.

Stories like this unfold every day in primary care offices across the country.

Primary care physicians have quietly become the front door to mental healthcare.

Most primary care physicians were trained to diagnose disease, manage chronic illness, prescribe medications, and coordinate medical care. They were not trained to provide psychotherapy or manage complex mental health disorders. Yet every day, they find themselves caring for patients whose physical health is profoundly influenced by their emotional well-being.

Whether they intended to or not, primary care physicians now practice at the intersection of medicine and mental health.

Consider a typical day in primary care, which often looks like a combination of a patient who presents with poorly controlled diabetes, another who struggles with chronic pain, a third who complains of persistent fatigue despite a normal medical workup, and others who report headaches, insomnia, or gastrointestinal discomfort that has resisted every diagnostic test.

Beneath many of the symptoms physicians treat every day lies another layer: stress, grief, anxiety, depression, loneliness, caregiver burden, trauma, and the daily challenges of sustaining healthy behavior.

Depression can undermine a person's ability to manage diabetes. Chronic stress contributes to hypertension and cardiovascular disease. Anxiety frequently presents through physical symptoms before patients recognize or feel comfortable discussing the emotional distress beneath them. Social isolation influences sleep, immune function, recovery from illness, and even mortality.

The complaint presented doesn’t always tell the whole story.

Primary care is often the place where physical symptoms become the language of psychological distress.

This is perhaps the first lesson every primary care physician should recognize. Psychological distress rarely arrives neatly labeled. It often lies in a layer beneath the physical symptoms that bring patients into the examination room.

Patients rarely schedule appointments with their primary care physicians, stating "I think I'm depressed and this is impacting my sleep," or "I'd like to discuss my anxiety and how it’s impacting my digestion." Instead, they describe fatigue, pain, dizziness, insomnia, gastrointestinal problems, or worsening chronic diseases. They speak the language of physical symptoms because that is what they believe is expected when visiting the doctor, and those are tangible, familiar, and often easier to discuss than emotional suffering.

Recognizing this pattern is not about turning primary care physicians into psychologists. It is about recognizing that understanding a patient's psychology often leads to a better understanding of their physiology. Looking beneath the symptoms frequently brings clinicians closer to the factors driving illness which saves them from promoting an intervention aimed solely at a physical manifestation.

One of the greatest strengths of primary care medicine is the continuity of relationships. Primary care physicians often know their patients over years or even decades. They witness life transitions, family changes, chronic illnesses, losses, and recoveries. That continuity creates the perfect opportunity for conversations about emotional well-being that might never occur in an acute/urgent healthcare setting.

For many, a visit to the primary care physician becomes the first place where they feel safe to acknowledge emotional distress. They may never schedule an appointment specifically to discuss depression or anxiety, but they may mention feeling exhausted during a diabetes follow-up, describe worsening sleep during an annual physical, or admit to feeling overwhelmed while discussing blood pressure management. The familiarity and trust established through an ongoing relationship often lower the barriers that prevent people from seeking mental health support elsewhere.

However, recognizing psychological distress is only the beginning. Helping patients successfully connect with appropriate care is an entirely different challenge. A referral may identify the next step, but it does not guarantee that the patient will take it. Access to mental healthcare is rarely limited by recognition alone. More often, it is limited by the complexity of navigating the healthcare system after the need has been identified. Long wait times, insurance limitations, transportation challenges, competing responsibilities, stigma, and the emotional burden of seeking help can all become obstacles between identifying a concern and receiving treatment.

This is where integrated care offers a meaningful advantage. Rather than viewing a referral as the endpoint of responsibility, integrated care seeks to shorten the distance between recognition and treatment. Whether through behavioral health professionals embedded within primary care practices, warm handoffs to mental health providers, collaborative care teams, or coordinated follow-up, the goal is not simply to identify psychological concerns. The goal is to ensure that patients receive the care they need.

Primary care physicians do not need to become mental health specialists.

They can leverage their already established relationship to become psychological sentinels.

Psychological sentinels are clinicians who recognize when emotional, behavioral, or social factors are influencing health. They initiate meaningful conversations, assess immediate needs, and connect patients with timely, coordinated support before psychological distress evolves into more significant illness.

Neither medicine nor psychology is sufficient on its own for dealing with chronic and persistent illnesses. Together they allow clinicians to treat not simply the disease, but the person living with it.

This is the basis of integrated health. Psychologists bring expertise in motivation, behavior change, resilience, communication, coping, and the social and emotional factors that shape health. Physicians bring expertise in diagnosis, medical management, and disease treatment. Together, they address not only disease but the person living with it.

Questions such as, "How have you been coping?" or "What has life been like since your symptoms began?" may reveal information that no laboratory test or imaging study can provide. More importantly, they communicate something every patient hopes to experience: I want to understand you, not just your symptoms.

Primary care, now and in the future, cannot be defined solely by earlier diagnoses, better medications, or more sophisticated technology. It should also be defined by the physicians’ willingness to recognize that every symptom has a story; every diagnosis exists within the context of a person's life, and every treatment plan succeeds or fails through human behavior.

Every patient who walks into a primary care office brings more than a diagnosis. They bring a story, a family, a history, relationships, and life experiences that shape their health in ways laboratory tests cannot measure.

Primary care physicians already understand much of this intuitively. The next evolution of healthcare is ensuring that our education, healthcare systems, and care models fully support that reality. This is the basis of integrated health education.

Mental health has never been separated from healthcare.

It has been quietly sitting in the waiting room all along.

item.title: Why Parenting Requires Regulating Ourselves First
item.description:
Parenting

Why Parenting Requires Regulating Ourselves First

Trauma symptoms and the postpartum maternal brain.

Posted July 9, 2026

Key points
  • Parenting often requires regulating our own emotions to effectively respond to our children.
  • Postpartum PTSD symptoms may affect brain regions involved in emotion regulation and caregiving.
  • Trauma symptoms can make early parenting harder, but support and treatment can help.
Source: Natalia Vladimirova / Unsplash

My daughter headed off for a week at sleepaway camp for the first time this week. I was excited for her and knew she would do great. She is brave and confident in a way I love and admire. Still, the goodbye hit me harder than I expected. In that moment, I was leaving my baby girl. Where had the time gone? I managed not to cry and kept my cool as she headed off to her swimming test without even looking back. As a parent, I knew that was exactly what I was supposed to do. My job was not to make my emotions the center of her experience. My job was to regulate myself enough to give her the freedom to have her own experience—to feel excited, nervous, proud, homesick, or whatever else came up for her.

And yet, it felt like just yesterday that she was a baby in my arms.

That moment at camp is just one version of a task parents face over and over: feeling our own emotions deeply while also needing to regulate them enough to make room for our children’s emotions and needs. This is not an easy task, and we don’t get to wait until our children are walking and talking to face it. This kind of emotion regulation begins much earlier, and we know it is especially relevant in early postpartum, when babies first begin learning their own regulation by tuning into their parent’s responses. Managing one’s own emotions is helpful for being able to offer warm, flexible, and attuned responses as a parent.

Source: Hollie Santos / Unsplash

In this time, new mothers are learning their babies’ cues, responding to varied needs, and at the same time recovering physically and sleeping very little. For many mothers, this is a period of love and early connection with baby, but it is also a period of vulnerability, especially for women struggling with mental health symptoms. While more awareness has emerged for depression and anxiety in the postpartum period, this is also a time of high vulnerability for posttraumatic stress symptoms, yet we know very little about the impacts of trauma symptoms in this time.

How Trauma Symptoms Affect the Maternal Brain

Our team at the Grady Trauma Project at Emory University has been working to better understand how posttraumatic stress symptoms may affect the maternal brain during this early postpartum period with the goal of identifying what kinds of supports may be most helpful and when. In a recent study led by Rebecca Lipschutz, trauma-exposed mothers came into the lab when their babies were 6-12 weeks old.(1) First, we observed mothers and babies during a caregiving interaction. Later, trained coders rated maternal sensitivity, representing how well mothers noticed and responded flexibly and warmly to their infants’ cues. A week or two later, mothers completed a functional magnetic resonance imaging scan (fMRI). During the scan, they listened to recordings of their own babies crying as well as control sounds. This allowed us to examine which parts of their brain were activated in response to their own infant’s distress.

Source: Jessica Hearn / Unsplash

We found that higher maternal sensitivity in the context of caregiving was related to greater activation in the insula, a brain region involved in noticing important emotional and bodily signals. In parenting, this may help mothers tune in to what their baby is communicating. Mothers with high levels of posttraumatic stress symptoms, however, showed more blunted activation in this region, along with other key regions, including the amygdala and the ventromedial prefrontal cortex. The amygdala helps detect threat and emotional salience, while the ventromedial prefrontal cortex helps regulate emotional responses and calm the body’s threat system. So, moms with high symptoms were showing reduced engagement in these emotion salience and regulation regions.

This does not mean mothers with posttraumatic stress symptoms cannot be sensitive, loving, responsive mothers. Many are extraordinarily attuned to their children. But it does mean that trauma symptoms can sometimes make the work of parenting harder, especially during a period already marked by stress, sleep deprivation, physical discomfort, and hormonal changes, all factors that can make emotion regulation even harder.

These findings also point toward hope. The postpartum period is a time of vulnerability, but it is also a time of remarkable capacity for change. If we can identify mothers who are struggling and connect them with effective support, we may be able to improve maternal well-being and support healthier parent-child relationships, which also helps children long-term.

Why Screening for PTSD and Trauma-Related Distress in New Mothers Matters

Evidence-based treatments that directly target posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), like trauma-focused cognitive-behavioral therapy, may be one important pathway. Treatments that strengthen emotion regulation, reduce physiological arousal, and help mothers respond to distress without becoming overwhelmed, such as mindfulness and emotion regulation skills-based interventions, may also be useful. But before any of that can happen, we have to identify who needs support. That is why screening for PTSD and trauma-related distress in the perinatal period matters. We routinely ask new mothers about depression, and that is essential. But for many women, trauma-related symptoms, such as intrusive memories of past trauma, avoidance, hypervigilance, or emotional numbing, may be a central part of their postpartum experience. When we fail to ask about trauma, we miss opportunities to help.

Watching my daughter walk away toward camp reminded me that parenting so often requires regulating ourselves first. That is true in big transitions, like saying goodbye at camp, but it is also true in the earliest days of motherhood, when a mother is learning to read her infant’s cues, respond to distress, and stay regulated enough to soothe. For many women, this work unfolds while they are also carrying trauma symptoms, stress, exhaustion, and physical recovery. Supporting mothers during this critical period is not optional. It is foundational to maternal mental health, to infant development, and to the well-being of families and communities.

If you are a mother in postpartum and feeling overwhelmed, you are not alone. Resources are available. Check out Postpartum Support International, and if you need immediate support, you can call or text the 988 lifeline. To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: Why Immigrant Children Can Feel Pressured to Preserve the Family Culture
item.description:
Cross-Cultural Psychology

Why Immigrant Children Can Feel Pressured to Preserve the Family Culture

When families see cultural preservation as a shared responsibility, everyone benefits.

Posted July 9, 2026

Key points
  • Children often become cultural carriers through everyday family life and traditions.
  • Cultural pride can become pressure when children feel preservation depends on them.
  • Shared family responsibility supports healthier identity development and belonging.
  • Culture thrives when it evolves across generations instead of resting on one child.

In many immigrant families, language, traditions, values, and family stories carry culture forward with care. Culture lives in the meals prepared at home, the holidays celebrated together, and the customs that connect one generation to the next.

But this inheritance can, over time, turn heavier. A child who hesitates before answering a grandparent in a fading language may already carry more than they realize. Without anyone asking them to do so, they may come to feel responsible for keeping their family's culture alive into the next generation.

This responsibility often develops gradually. Children recognize the sacrifices their parents made to build a new life. They notice the growing distance between their home culture and the surrounding society and come to understand that some traditions may fade without continued practice. While maintaining cultural connections can strengthen identity and family relationships, some children come to believe that preserving those connections depends on them alone.

This experience matters because cultural preservation can become both a source of pride and a source of pressure.

How Children Become Cultural Carriers

Children often become "cultural carriers" through everyday family life. No one sits them down or assigns formal expectations—instead, parents may encourage them to speak a heritage language at home, participate in cultural celebrations, learn traditional customs, or stay connected with relatives who live far away. These experiences help children understand their family's history and take pride in their cultural identity.

For immigrant families, these traditions often take on added meaning. Living in a new country can make families more intentional about preserving the customs, values, and language that connect them to their roots. Children may recognize that their experiences differ from their parents’ and grandparents’, placing them at the intersection of two cultural worlds.

Over time, many children begin to see themselves as more than participants in these traditions. They become the family member who remembers holiday rituals, teaches younger siblings cultural practices, or helps keep the heritage language alive at home. These roles often emerge naturally and can strengthen their sense of belonging within the family.

In time, cultural preservation may begin to feel less like a shared family practice and more like a personal duty. What begins as inheritance can gradually become something children feel they must carry forward alone.

Why Some Children Feel More Responsible Than Others

Some children naturally become cultural ambassadors within their families and communities. They may feel comfortable explaining family traditions to friends, participating in cultural events, or helping younger siblings understand their heritage. Others become the primary heritage-language speakers within the family, especially if they spend more time with grandparents or relatives less proficient in the dominant language.

Birth order can also shape these experiences. Older siblings may feel responsible for modeling cultural values or helping younger family members stay connected to traditions. Conscientious children, or those highly attuned to family expectations, may internalize cultural responsibility more deeply than their siblings.

Family dynamics further influence these roles. Some families openly stress the importance of preserving traditions, while others convey these values more subtly through everyday interactions. However expressed, children often absorb them because they care about their family relationships.

Becoming a cultural carrier is not inherently a problem. Many children find meaning and confidence in maintaining connections to their heritage. The trouble starts when children believe the work falls on them alone, when in truth, it belongs to the whole family and community.

When Cultural Preservation Becomes Pressure

Cultural connection can become stressful when children begin to feel solely responsible for keeping it alive. Even children who value their heritage deeply can grow anxious about whether they are doing enough to preserve it.

Some children carry a secret guilt when they lose proficiency in a heritage language, drift away from traditions, or embrace aspects of another culture. Others worry that they are disappointing their family when they can no longer fully take part in once-familiar customs. These concerns often go unspoken, yet they shape how children see themselves and their culture.

Many immigrant-origin children grow up balancing the expectations of home with the realities of school, friendships, and the broader society. As they adapt to new environments, some cultural practices naturally change. The fear of disappointing family, or of being blamed for letting the culture slip away, can linger beneath the surface for years. What begins as connection can gradually feel like obligation, leaving children caught between honoring their heritage and simply growing up.

The Impact on Identity Development

Adolescence is a period of identity exploration, when young people begin to understand who they are and who they hope to become. For children growing up in immigrant families, this process often includes learning how to integrate multiple cultural influences into a coherent sense of self.

When cultural preservation becomes central to self-worth, identity development grows more complicated. A child might want to try a new interest or express themselves differently. But they hesitate, worrying it might look like they are turning their back on where they came from. They may question whether adapting to their surrounding environment makes them less connected to their heritage.

Research consistently shows that children benefit from bicultural identities, valuing both heritage culture and the broader society they live in. When these identities feel compatible rather than competing, they support psychological well-being and a stronger sense of belonging.

Children who feel solely responsible for preserving culture experience tension between authenticity and obligation. They feel they must choose between personal growth and cultural loyalty. This pressure can complicate identity development, when identity needs room to evolve alongside changing experience.

Supporting Culture Without Creating Burden

Cultural continuity is strongest when children feel invited to participate. Families can share cultural traditions across generations instead of resting them on one child’s shoulders.

Parents can help by explaining the meaning behind traditions, sharing family stories, and giving children room to take part. When children understand why certain customs matter, they develop genuine appreciation rather than a sense of obligation.

Culture also evolves naturally. Families adapt traditions, languages shift across generations, and children develop identities shaped by both their heritage and the society in which they live. These changes do not signal cultural loss. Instead, they show how culture continues to grow in new contexts.

Letting children engage with culture in their own way supports both connection and healthy development. Families can emphasize shared values, relationships, and belonging, rather than measuring commitment by flawless language proficiency or strict adherence to every tradition.

When cultural preservation becomes a collective family effort, children stay connected to their heritage with pride.

Conclusion

Culture is not preserved by one child alone. It continues through families, communities, and generations sharing stories, traditions, values, and language over time. Children play an important role in this process, but they should not feel that the future of their heritage depends entirely on them.

When families approach cultural continuity as a shared and evolving process, children stay connected to their roots while remaining free to define themselves. In doing so, cultural preservation becomes less about carrying a burden and more about participating in a living tradition that grows alongside each new generation.

item.title: The Cultural Evolution of Calorie Recommendations
item.description:
Memes

The Cultural Evolution of Calorie Recommendations

How the 2,000 kcal/day meme was born and grew up.

Posted July 9, 2026

Key points
  • The meme is Earth’s second replicator, evolving, as the gene does, via replication, variation, and selection.
  • The idea that we should eat 2,000 calories a day dates to 1993 and has proven a remarkably successful meme.
  • The 2k meme has spread via cultural niche construction and human behaviour, identity, and cognitive bias.

This post is Part 3 of a series. Part 1 can be found here, and Part 2 can be found here.

Ideas and habits spread amongst humans for many reasons, many of which have little to do with whether they are good for us or not. In this series, we’re looking at how numerical the Western world has made eating and exercise. A touch of cultural evolution theory may help us think about how and why this trend might have spread other than “because it’s a good thing.”

Everyone knows about one of the replicators this planet is home to: the gene. A simple “evolutionary algorithm” acts on genetic material via the mind-bending power of its three-step process: replication, variation, and selection. The brilliance of Darwin’s realization was that when these three steps occur, design must arise—with no need for a designer. Philosopher Dan Dennett (1995) called this “the single best idea anyone ever had.”

Not so many people know about the second replicator alive and kicking on this planet: the meme. It’s funny how the idea of internet memes took the technical term and kept the idea of information spreading like a virus but lost the link to how the spreading happens: via the evolutionary algorithm. The term was coined at the end of Richard Dawkins’ (1976) The Selfish Gene to designate a unit of cultural transmission subject to the same evolutionary process as the gene:

Examples of memes are tunes, ideas, catch-phrases, clothes fashions, and ways of making pots or of building arches. Just as genes propagate themselves in the gene pool by leaping from body to body via sperm or eggs, so memes propagate themselves in the meme pool by leaping from brain to brain, via a process which, in the broad sense, can be called imitation.

Memetics is the study of this second replicator. In the realm of ideas and habits, we humans like to imagine that we are the designers, making usually good decisions for usually good reasons. But if we take the meme’s-eye view, we look not like clever designers with foresight and purpose, but instead like the lumbering hosts on which innumerable circulating memes are trying to find a home before getting themselves passed on again. Like any replicator, memes will get themselves copied when they can, regardless of the benefits or harms to either the genes or the organisms.

Let’s take one of the memes introduced in part 2: the idea that 2,000 calories is a good amount to aim to eat every day. As I outlined, this notion has gained traction via a messy mixture of (1) dietary self-report of questionable accuracy plus (2) rounding down to ensure that postmenopausal women wouldn’t be encouraged to eat more—and, crucially, to make it simple and memorable.

In 1993, when the decision about the daily calorie standard was being made, U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) dietary intake surveys of the time had generated a value of 2,350 as the average daily calorie consumption reported. Even this higher value was probably lower than true average needs (Redman et al., 2013). But the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) rejected the idea of using 2,350 as the daily recommended allowance. They also rejected the idea of trusting the public with a range (1,600 to 2,200 for women, 2,000 to 3,000 for men—again, for women already lower than available data suggested). Instead, they opted for a number that was and remains “much lower than either measurements or estimates of the total energy needs of all but the smallest and most sedentary people” (Nestle & Nesheim, 2012).

The rationale for the choice was explicitly memetic: The people at the FDA decided (as Nestle and Nesheim put it) that 2,000 was “easier to use” than 2,350 and therefore “a better tool for nutrition education.” The 2k meme won out, and it has done a good job of winning out ever since—even though, as I’ll argue later in this series, it has done so much harm.

4 Contributors to the Success of the 200-Calorie Meme

The 2k meme has probably achieved memetic success by routes other than numerical simplicity. Here are four likely contributors:

  1. Environment: The 2,000-calorie meme has altered its cultural environment in a way that makes it more likely to be copied. As soon as the FDA decided on 2,000, they knew that they would need to encourage people to use the number by putting calorie and other nutritional information everywhere, which meant working out in enormous detail everything from standard serving sizes to font sizes in a nearly 900-page Federal Register notice about labelling regulations, plus a long guide to reading the nutritional facts panel. They went so far as to specify, for example, that on food packaging, “Calories must be in a type size no smaller than 8 point.” All of this apparatus, already labyrinthine in 1993, has mushroomed to unimagined scope by 2026, from commercial food testing labs generating macro- and micronutrient evaluations to smartphone algorithms combining basal metabolic rate (BMR) estimates and heart-rate measurements into energy expenditure graphs. The existence of a 2k target claiming global applicability encourages the proliferation of these technologies of quantification.
  2. Behaviour: In turn, the tech shapes our habits, encouraging us to eat less or giving us licence to “indulge.” As Sue Blackmore’s book The Meme Machine (1999) explores, the meme is protected by the behaviours that it induces in us. The 2k meme uses our behaviours (turning the packet over, choosing the option that has the fewest calories, buying the watch with the most accurate readings, skipping lunch before a dinner out…) to copy itself: to create more iterations of itself in the world and increase the likelihood that more will be created in the future. And as I’ll explore later, many of these behaviours tend in the direction of disordered eating.
  3. Identity: All these everyday behaviours get reinforced by, and in turn reinforce, identity-related belief systems about being the kind of person who does this—who doesn’t overeat, who takes care of their body, who cares about their health. The primary guide for eating and movement behaviours has shifted from instincts to numbers—and we can now reframe this power shift as one from humans’ experience to memes’ replicator power. Counter-movements have arisen—intuitive eating emphasises attunement to hunger/satiety signals, for example—but they’re not mainstream. Human experiences and thus identities are, en masse, far more profoundly driven by the memes than even 20 years ago, let alone 200.
  4. Cognitive bias: In some ways, we’re wired to be defenceless. For human minds, for example, precision is easily confused with accuracy: in “precision bias,” a more specific number is assumed to be more correct. So if your watch or your phone spits out a number at you—let’s say, 2689—and says that’s how much energy you used today, you’re inclined to infer that the number reflects reality in a reliable way. Maybe that’s also why the FDA rejected the idea of a range: It sounds like there’s less conviction behind it. This is a paradoxical flipside of the choice of 2k for memorability: We like (remember) round numbers for our rules, but we like (trust) un-round numbers for our measuring. Remembering that, precision aside, inaccuracy is at the heart of both may be one way to help reduce the unhelpful kinds of power they can have over us.

item.title: Surprising Mental Health Effects of GLP-1 Weight Loss Drugs
item.description:
Psychiatry

Surprising Mental Health Effects of GLP-1 Weight Loss Drugs

GLP-1 medications may be used to treat select psychiatric disorders.

Posted July 9, 2026

Key points
  • GLP-1 drugs are showing promise as part of a treatment plan for some mental health disorders.
  • There is more research data about GLP-1 use for depression and substance use disorders than other disorders.
  • GLP-1 drugs should not be used for eating disorders except when part of a research trial.
Young woman eating junk food.
Source: StockSnap / Pixabay

GLP-1 medications are effective for the treatment of overweight, obesity, and type 2 diabetes. Emerging evidence has suggested that the GLP-1 medications may also be useful for the treatment of some psychiatric disorders.

People with diabetes and/or obesity "have an elevated risk of developing depression, anxiety, and suicide" (Taipale, 2026). There is good evidence that GLP-1 drugs can improve these co-morbid conditions in some patients.

GLP-1 is a hormone secreted from the intestinal tract triggered by eating food. It stimulates insulin release from the pancreas, slows stomach emptying, and makes people feel full.

GLP-1 is also produced in the brain and affects nerve function, "energy balance, appetite regulation, and brain rewards from food and drug intake" (Angarita, 2021). It also decreases inflammation and oxidative stress, which are implicated in the development of depression and anxiety (Gunturu, 2024).

Depression

Several studies "show improvement in depression symptoms following treatment with GLP-1" (Gunturu, 2024). For example, one study showed a significant reduction in depression scores in subjects taking GLP-1 compared to subjects taking a placebo (Chen, 2024).

In addition to improvements in depressive symptoms, GLP-1 has "been shown to have neuroprotective...properties" (Cooper, 2023).

In contrast, one research trial using GLP-1 drugs on obese research subjects did not show a benefit from GLP-1 in the prevention of depression, anxiety, and suicidal behavior (Kornelius, 20240). However, this study did not address whether the depressive subjects improved on these medications.

When GLP-1 drugs were first released, the FDA did surveillance for possible negative side effects. There was early evidence suggesting that suicidal ideation and behavior were more common among people taking these drugs. However, new data convinced the FDA that GLP-1 does not increase the risk of suicidal ideation or behavior (Drug Safety Communication, 2026).

An example of research supporting the FDA's new position is a study showing GLP-1 is "not associated with an increased risk of psychiatric adverse events or worsening depression symptoms" (Pierret, 2025).

Substance Use Disorders

Evidence supports the use of GLP-1 medications for "treating alcohol and other substance use disorders" (Farokhnia, 2026). This is not surprising because GLP-1 medications "inhibit dopamine release in the brain's reward center" (Laurindo, 2022).

Alcohol use disorder treatment by GLP-1 medication is the best studied of the chemical addictions. In one study, "low dose semaglutide reduced the amount of alcohol consumed, fewer drinks per day, and decreased weekly craving" (Hendershot, 2025).

In another study, a GLP-1 drug "significantly reduced heavy drinking days and total alcohol intake in a subset of obese patients" (Klausen, 2022). In this study, only obese research subjects had a reduction in alcohol use.

Overall, it appears that overweight, obese, and/or diabetic research subjects have better results than normal-weight subjects when using a GLP-1 medication to treat a substance use disorder (Marquez-Meneses, 2025).

In addition to alcohol use disorder, other substances have also been studied, "such as psychostimulants, opioids, and nicotine" (Bruns, 2024). Nicotine addiction from smoking and vaping is an ongoing public health challenge. Stopping smoking can be challenging. "One major barrier to long-term smoking abstinence is body weight gain during withdrawal" (Herman, 2024).

Studies have shown that GLP-1 reduces the voluntary use of nicotine and prevents withdrawal-induced overeating and weight gain (Herman, 2024). Also, evidence suggests that "GLP-1 improves cognitive deficits, as well as depressive- and anxiety-like behaviors, which contribute to smoking relapse during withdrawal" (Herman, 2024).

Eating Disorders

Binge eating disorder (BED) is the most common specific eating disorder (Himmerich, 2024). "BED is frequently associated with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, depression, bipolar disorder, anxiety disorders, alcohol and nicotine use disorder, and obesity" (Himmerich, 2024).

Although the role of GLP-1 medication in the treatment of BED is not established, research has shown that these medications reduce "binge eating in individuals with obesity or overweight" (Himmerich, 2024). Also, research suggests that there may be neuropsychiatric effects from GLP-1 use that provide risk reduction for binge eating disorder (Choudhury, 2026).

Unfortunately, some individuals use GLP-1 medications "to maintain their eating disorders (e.g., anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, and binge eating disorder) through rapid dietary restriction and weight loss" (Peiper, 2026). This is an unsafe practice and should not be done.

Weight Gain from Antidepressants and Antipsychotics

Weight gain is a well-known side effect of many of these medications. Some people stop taking their medication because of weight gain.

There are recommendations for pharmacologic treatment of weight gain from these medications. For example, one recommendation is to add "metformin or GLP-1" drugs to manage weight gain from these drugs (Solmi, 2024; Mouawad, 2025).

In one study, GLP-1 was given for 30 weeks to patients with schizophrenia who had prediabetes and obesity. The results showed that the treatment "was safe, lowered blood glucose and weight" (average loss of 20.3 pounds), "and improved physical quality of life without worsening mental health" (Ganeshalingam, 2025).

Anxiety Disorders

There is less human research on the use of GLP-1 medications to help manage anxiety. Good studies of animals given GLP-1 have shown "consistent reduction in anxiety-like behavior and improved biological markers related to stress resilience, while clinical cohorts (i.e., human studies) demonstrated mixed but suggestive evidence of reduced anxiety incidence and lower suicidal ideation risk" (Yi, 2026).

The Bottom Line

GLP-1 medications are evolving as a potential treatment for several mental health disorders. Depression and substance use disorders have more data than others. More extensive studies are needed before a definitive recommendation can be made for when and how to use GLP-1 medications and what dose is optimal for this purpose.

item.title: Human Collaboration Has a Vital Negativity That AI Does Not
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Human Collaboration Has a Vital Negativity That AI Does Not

Relationships exert influence through negative nonverbal cues. AI does not, yet.

Posted July 9, 2026

Key points
  • Strong relationships exert influence in an unusual way, through negative nonverbal cues and muttered asides.
  • Relational collaborators signal, suggest, and sometimes deliberately move our behavior through discomfort.
  • The signals that shape us in human collaboration are absent while working with an AI model alone.

Working relationships are not productive simply because colleagues share sustained positive feedback. Strong relationships exert influence in an unusual way, through negative nonverbal cues, dismissive gestures, and muttered asides. That is the real stuff of work that ultimately helps create something of value.

How Subtle Reactions Shape Decision-Making in Teams

The people we work with and trust do not simply tell us what to do; they shape our choices through reactions we absorb: a colleague's slight hesitation, a mentor's shift in tone, the meaningful shrug. We often revise our thinking, our decisions, and our actions in response to these signals, which carry meaning as vivid as the spoken message. Research on nonverbal behavior bears this out. Ambady and Rosenthal found that brief samples of a person's expressive behavior—the face, the posture, the tone—carry enough information for observers to make accurate judgments about that person, often more reliably than words do.

Relational collaborators signal, suggest, and sometimes deliberately move our behavior through discomfort. A graphic designer I am working with can show unhappiness with a choice I have made, and that reaction leads me to reconsider and often to change the decision. Part of this is due to the designer's professional skill, but a great part of it is relational. The disapproval carries weight because it comes from a person whose judgment I have come to trust and whose regard I would rather keep than lose.

The same holds when working with a software developer, a writer, or a key advisor. The dynamic runs in reverse as well. I might show unhappiness, consciously or not, and the other person reads it, weighs where it is coming from, mulls it over, and adjusts. A collaborator's displeasure moves us more than the same collaborator's praise, given the higher weight that negative signals typically carry.

Nonverbal Cues And Relational Collaborations
Source: Deepak Sirdeshmukh

Behavioral science supports the dynamics I am describing. When I change a decision to relieve a collaborator's expressed displeasure, that is negative reinforcement, an operant process in which a behavior that removes an unpleasant state is strengthened. Mowrer's two-factor theory suggests that anticipatory behavior requires both classical and operant processes working together. Classical conditioning first associates the unease with a cue, and operant conditioning then rewards the action that relieves the unease. What gets reinforced is not the removal of the displeasure itself, which may never arrive, but the relief from anticipating it.

Bandura's social cognitive theory points to similar outcomes but stemming from expectations formed in advance. For Bandura, we do not simply absorb consequences; we form expectations about what an action will produce, and we act on those expectations before any consequence materializes. We also learn by watching a person we regard, modeling their judgment rather than waiting to be rewarded or corrected. When I anticipate a developer’s reaction and adjust before suggesting an update to a project, I am acting on an expectancy built from a relationship, not responding to a stimulus in front of me.

The Absence of Relational Dynamics in Collaboration With AI Models

These complex dynamics, often carried in nonverbal negative signals, are the part that has gone missing when I work with a large language model. The models have added efficiency and creativity to a variety of tasks in ways I had not anticipated. That said, no matter how much I invite the model to push back, in the end it supports the choice I have already made, or it has no real stake in the choice at all. The signals that shape me in human collaboration, often delivered as asides and often persisting long after a decision or discussion, are absent. There is no displeasure to relieve, no regard to keep, no relationship in which my choice carries any weight for the other party.

Some aspects might get captured as multimodal artificial intelligence becomes commonplace: systems that pair language with video, expressive on-screen avatars, physical robots. A pause, a change in tone, a shift in what is visible on a screen could all be simulated to show something like displeasure.

What cannot be manufactured is the relational core of the exchange, the fact that the other person's regard is real and that I stand to keep it or lose it. Baumeister and Leary argued that the need to belong, to form and keep interpersonal attachments, is a fundamental human motivation, and that the prospect of losing an attachment moves us on its own. This is why a collaborator's regard has force. It is not merely information about my choices; it is a bond I would rather not damage.

That is one reason I keep a trusted person involved in any work I do with a model rather than work with the model alone. The pushback, the frown over a Zoom call, the shrug emoji in a text—all of these exert powerful influence on collaborations and the outcomes they reach. It may be another reason working with people continues to matter, even as the tools grow more capable and more human-like.

item.title: Got Relationship Stress? Take the Ocean View
item.description:
Stress

Got Relationship Stress? Take the Ocean View

Five steps for gaining perspective when stress gets the better of you.

Posted July 9, 2026

Key points
  • When in the grips of stress, we lose our ability for seeing a big picture and get stuck in "small self-view."
  • When we get stuck in small self-view during relationship conflict, we lose capacity for perspective taking.
  • Learning how to take the "Ocean View" allows for more flexible and expansive thinking and for connection.
Source: Openclipart-Vectors / Pixabay

Several months ago I watched captivated as the Artemis II capsule catapulted through the Earth’s atmosphere at 25,000 miles per hour, was enveloped by temperatures of 10,000 degrees Celsius, and splashed down into the Pacific Ocean, bringing its four astronauts safely home after traveling farther from Earth than any human has done. Nothing like a little space travel to put things into perspective.

On my morning walk the next day, I was greeted by both the rising sun and the crescent moon, and I thought about the magnificent photos of the moon and Earth taken from outer space on this latest space excursion. I am, after all, just a speck in a cosmic universe.

That shift of perspective is so counter to what I, and most of us humans, experience much of the time. This is especially so when in the grips of stress. It is what I call the “small self-view.” Opposite to seeing the big picture and putting things in a wider frame, we see things from the perspective of me, myself, and I. This can be especially unhelpful and present obstacles when it comes to relationships. When caught in the small self-view in the midst of stress or interpersonal conflict, this narrow focus and tunnel vision can limit our thinking and behavioral repertoire in ways that can often make it hard to see the other’s perspective.

In the grips of stress (when our nervous system perceives “threat” of some kind), it makes sense that our body mobilizes into this survival state. If I’m running from a tiger, I don’t have the luxury of taking in the surroundings, the periphery, the expansive sky, or the flowers growing in the far-off field. My body, flooded with stress chemicals, wants to do one thing, and that is to survive by fighting or escaping. Those Stone Age ancestors who stopped to ponder a bigger picture or notice the flowers likely didn’t live long enough to pass their genes on to us.

How to Know if You’re in Small Self-View

Some signs of small self-view include body constriction, tightening, tense muscles, shallow breathing, narrow focus of attention, feeling defensive in an interaction (like you need to protect yourself), tunnel vision, and inability to see a bigger picture.

This is not “bad.” Sometimes this state can be necessary and adaptive (especially if there is a true threat of some kind). But much of the time we can benefit from a more expansive vantage point.

Enter the "Ocean View"

Imagine looking out at the ocean. From the perspective of the wave, it may think of itself as a single, isolated wave; but you, the onlooker, can see that that wave is connected to and part of the vast ocean. The wave is just a small part of something much more expansive and interconnected.

When we can take the Ocean View, this offers us a great deal more cognitive and behavioral flexibility (we can see things from the widest perspective and make choices that may not otherwise feel accessible when locked in a narrow mindset).

The Ocean View, which I write about in my book You Don’t Have to Change to Change Everything, is not just a shift in perspective but, importantly, a shift in physiology. When our nervous system is in a state of greater regulation and balance, the sympathetic branch of our nervous system works in harmony with the parasympathetic branch (mediated by the ventral branch of our vagus nerve). There is a natural shift in perspective when this occurs. From a nervous system grounded in safety, our stress response dials down, and we have access to a bigger picture. The world looks different. There is more possibility for connection and seeing other points of view.

Think about being really angry at someone and believing it’s your way or the highway. Then, when you cool down, you realize there are other ways of looking at the situation and maybe things aren’t as all-or-nothing as you thought.

Stepping Out of Small Self-View Into the Ocean View

1. Think about some typical moments when you get caught in small self-view. Perhaps it’s when yelling at your teenager to do something you’ve asked them to do 10 times already, or in an argument with your partner, or at work when that particular coworker pushes your buttons, or when you just have way too much to do and are running around in a state of frenzy.

2. Notice what small self-view feels like. Bring awareness to your body. Do you feel tight, constricted, tense? Is your breathing shallow? What thoughts are going through your mind? Are those thoughts exaggerated, extreme, distorted, or self-focused? What emotions are present? Can you just name what is there (anger, frustration, anxiety, irritation, or something else) without judgment? Noticing and naming in this way can help dial down our inner alarm system.

3. Take a minute to do something to help calm and regulate your nervous system. See what it might need. If you are very tense and agitated, sometimes lightly shaking the body can help (e.g., lightly bouncing on your heels as you gently shake your legs, arms, hands, and shoulders to release tension).

For many people, regulating one’s breathing is a very effective way to activate the vagus nerve and parasympathetic branch of the nervous system. In particular, gentle inhalations through your nose and long, slow exhalations (try exhaling through your mouth) can be helpful.

Other forms of nervous system regulation might include pausing to bring awareness to your five senses and naming five objects you see, four things you can hear, and three things you can touch, two things you can smell, and one thing you can taste. Or, you might go to a nearby window and shift your visual field so you are gazing out at the horizon or the farthest things that you can see. These can have a calming effect on your nervous system.

As another strategy to try, directing visual attention to green elements in nature (such as looking at a tree) has been shown to reduce anxiety and increase well-being.

4. Once you notice a shift in your nervous system and begin to feel more settled, grounded, aware, calmer, etc., imagine taking a helicopter view of the situation you are in. From this vantage point, what can you notice that you might not have noticed before?

Using the examples from question one above, perhaps you notice that your teenager is sad and moody because things aren’t going well for them socially, and their shutting you out is a byproduct of their nervous system shutting down to protect themselves. Or you see that your partner may not have done this thing to intentionally upset you, or you wonder if your coworker might be dealing with some personal challenge outside of work that is causing a lot of inner suffering for them. If you have been running around in a frenzy and are on a short fuse, maybe you can see more clearly from this helicopter view what the biggest priorities are and what you might be able to let go for today.

5. Consider how you want to move forward into the next moments of your day. Ask yourself what you could choose that would align with who you want to be and what values are important to you. Taking a values-based perspective helps to further activate parts of the brain that turn down stress and lower cortisol levels in the body. In the example of the parent and teenager, focusing on being a parent who fosters and models healthy communication might just help shift the way you approach your teen to create a more win-win situation, both short-term and long-term.

As human beings who experience stress, we commonly fall into small self-view time and again. Learning to take an Ocean View not only helps expand our perspective; it may also enrich our relationships and help us feel more connected and interconnected to the people around us and to this vast planet on which we live.

item.title: How to Respond When an Adult Child Says "You Ruined My Life"
item.description:
Parenting

How to Respond When an Adult Child Says "You Ruined My Life"

What to say to an angry adult child and why it works.

Posted July 9, 2026

Key points
  • What you say to an angry adult child in the first 60 seconds matters most.
  • For parents, over-apologizing and defending themselves will backfire.
  • Three scripts can help parents validate pain without owning blame.

You tell yourself this time with your adult child is going to be a time of connection and positivity—and then, wham!—those painful words arrive without much warning. The parents I see for coaching recount Sunday dinner meltdowns, heated phone calls, or incendiary texts. For sure, I have heard stories of drama and pain during holiday gatherings and even weddings.

The words "You ruined my life," or similarly hurtful phrases, can rip your heart out as a parent. Based on my sessions with many struggling adult children, they are feeling a lot of pain and overwhelming emotions when they say those words. In the moment, parents tend to freeze up and default to one of two failing responses: They either collapse into an apology (I often hear from parents accused of "weaponizing" their tears) or they harden their defense. But neither of these responses meaningfully lowers the overall tension or lessens the fighting.

What to Say That Actually Works and Why

After a few decades of coaching families laden with emotional reactivity, I have found that what parents say in the first 60 seconds often matters more than anything they say afterward. Here are three responses that actually open the door to calmer, constructive conversations rather than impulsively slamming one shut.

"You Sound Really Hurt and in a Lot of Pain. Tell Me More."

Contrary to what many parents may believe (and I can see how it can feel counterintuitive), when you first acknowledge your adult child's pain—and that does mean you agree with their total perception—it can help both of you regulate your emotions. This type of response conveys that you can feel their hurt without needing to fix or refute it immediately. Many adult children aren't testing your guilt; they are testing whether you can stay present.

"I Hear That You Are Really Angry With Me"

The more you realize that anger is a surface emotion—with deeper ones such as frustration, shame, anxiety, and sadness lurking beneath—the easier it is not to be as rattled by it. Along these lines, anger at this often reflects a fear of disconnection. The more you can calmly acknowledge and hold a space for their anger, without apologizing, the more opportunity it creates to show that your relationship can hold hard feelings without breaking. Then you can calmly model constructive dialogue by saying something like, "Would you agree that if we can get to a place to talk about this calmly and constructively, it'll help us both get to a better place?"

"I Love You, and I'm Not Going to Accept Blame for Your Whole Life"

As I describe in my new book, You Ruined My Life—Now You Owe Me, the topic of over-the-top, misplaced blame frequently comes up when I work with parents and adult children. When adult children cast blame for their struggles on their parents, it converts (within the parents' mind) into incessant guilt. This blame-guilt cycle does not bode well for constructive dialogue and problem-solving. The statement, "I love you, and I'm not going to accept blame for your whole life," is the heart of what I call moving from fixer to coach. The fixer says, "Let me make this right for you." Yet when you say something like, "I believe you can work through this, and I am still here," you shift into a more effective coach/mentor mindset.

The Takeaway

The above soundbites are not meant to serve as a rigid script but as tools for adopting a mindset that is calmer and firmer, yet non-controlling. These phrases are meant to help you stay calm, connected, and constructive rather than reactive, defensive, or shutting down.

item.title: The Asterisk Version of Family
item.description:
Family Dynamics

The Asterisk Version of Family

The hidden struggles and emotional complexities of sperm and egg double donation.

Posted July 9, 2026

Key points
  • Double donation challenges our deepest assumptions about family and genetics.
  • Couples face questions, double binds, and uncertainty that few people understand.
  • Belonging grows through lived experience, not shared DNA.
Source: Giovanni Cancemi/Shutterstock

A double donation of sperm and eggs; a baby carried by the intended mother and raised by the intended parents, but genetically not related to either of them.

You've probably met a family built through double donation, but would you know?

More of these families exist now than at any point in history.

We don't even know how many double-donor families there are. But we do know this: in the UK, one of the few countries that keeps track, double-donor cycles have increased dramatically since 1991 (Human Fertilisation and Embryology Authority [HFEA], 2021). The US doesn't track these families at all (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention [CDC], 2024). And in lots of countries, creating embryos this way is not even legal (International Federation of Fertility Societies [IFFS], 2021).

Double donation challenges one of our deepest assumptions about what makes a family a family: genetics. It stretches us enough to come to terms with egg or sperm donation alone, so the loss of both is harder. More confronting, as they don't fit into the stories we traditionally tell ourselves about families.

The Asterisk Version

Our society only counts what it has a conceptual category for. You've seen it in the school family tree project. In the term 'real' as in real mother, or real father. Our culture treats genes as the gold standard of belonging. Everything else? A workaround.

"I tried to explain it to my great aunt, who told me it's very unnatural. Well, I suppose... I mean, yes, I feel so embarrassed." —Rachaeli and Simon*

Double-donor families disrupt the genetic model of family so completely that culturally, we have still to develop a space for them. Society places an asterisk beside these families as if they are somehow so completely different from the rest of us that they don't fit in. The asterisk version is true or real, but with an exception. Surely we can do better.

No Language for This

We rarely talk about the multitude of complexities these families face.

"Friends and family look at us like, is there even a point?

Jake's dealing with his own shame about his sperm count. He says at least I get to carry the baby, and that legitimizes it. He has no genes and no pregnancy. He struggles with his role. He feels like he won't see me or himself in a child, and so it's just his presence. Is that enough?

On his dark days, he says, 'Will I just be a cash cow to the child?' He knows that's not true.

This is our only chance. Do we not take it because of all the stuff that comes with it?" —Roni and Jake*

*Details changed for privacy.

The Questions

In single donation, one parent acts as the genetic bridge between the child and family. In double donation, that bridge disappears and the couple has to build 'belonging' without it.

Here's some of what Roni and Jake were grappling with:

If we're genetically unrelated, will we still feel like the parents?

Will we feel sad when we look at our child and see neither of us?

Will carrying the baby make Roni feel more like a parent than Jake?

What makes Jake the father when he has neither genes nor anything to outwardly show?

The Bind

Double donation creates numerous double binds.

Tell people what you are going through, and you invite opinions. Keep it private, and you reinforce shame (Slade et al., 2007).

Acknowledge that one parent carries the baby while the other has neither genes nor pregnancy, and you risk widening the gap. Ignore it, and one parent may feel isolated.

Look for yourself in your child, and you won't find either parent. Tell yourself that genetics do not matter, and you deny your losses.

Move forward, and you carry uncertainty about what this family will feel like. Walk away, and you may give up your only chance to become parents.

The Binds Are Real

There are two forces operating in these binds: societal pressure and internal psychological conflict, with the former impinging on the latter.

Society's investment in genetics is really about the existential fear of continuity ending. And, of course, the intended parents have also drunk the Kool-Aid. They, too, grew up believing that genes mean continuation, that we live on through our children. So when that ends, society's discomfort meets their own. The judgment comes from outside but finds its landing spot internally. Instead of questioning what society taught them about genes, they begin questioning themselves. Shame reverberates.

It is worth noting that we do this in many areas of life, from academic success to career, marriage, and parenthood. We absorb society’s definition of what success should look like, then blame ourselves when our lives don’t fit it.

Don't drink the Kool-Aid. Or at least spit some of it out.

Living Without Answers

Answers would be great, but how can you fully know the answers to these questions without living the experience?

What Roni and Jake wanted when they came to me was to be rid of the fear and have a concrete plan. But underneath was a much deeper question: How can we move forward with this level of fear? Does the fear signal that we can't do this? And how do we cope with so much uncertainty?

That became the real focus of our work. We explored coping styles, what they had drawn on in the past to get through difficult situations, and the inner resources they already possessed. It wasn't just what they thought, but how they responded to those thoughts.

The real shift came when they accepted that they didn't have all the answers, but recognized they still wanted this child.

Keeping why they wanted this child at the center became important. Maintaining a laser-like focus on that helped balance the fear and guide their thoughts and actions.

In practice, when the fear got overwhelming they circled back to their central question: do we still want this child? The answer was always yes. So the fear didn't have to leave, it just didn't have to drive the bus.

Roni and Jake now have a child conceived through double donation, and the joy outweighs the complicated, and sometimes crazy, questions they receive from others.

What Is Actually True

I know you know that genes do not decide who gets up at 3 a.m. time and again, for 18 years and beyond. So, I won't preach to the choir. And the research says the same. Families formed through third-party reproduction did not interfere with positive parent-child relationships (Golombok et al., 2023).

One thing I have noticed in the parent-child relationship is a kind of sixth sense that develops between parent and child. Perhaps it comes from noticing subtle shifts in tone, expression, or body language (Feldman, 2007). Parents know things about their children that others simply don't. This happens regardless of genetic connection. They are the hallmarks of true connection and intimacy. They quietly say: I see you and I know you.

item.title: 5 Habits to Build Lasting Happiness Into Your Life
item.description:
Happiness

5 Habits to Build Lasting Happiness Into Your Life

Social fitness, time affluence, and nature are key for a happy life.

Posted July 9, 2026

Source: Vitaly Gariev / Unsplash

Most people think of happiness as a feeling: something that arrives when conditions are right and fades when they’re not. But the last decade of psychological science tells a different story. Happiness isn’t primarily a mood state. It’s an output that emerges from the way your life is structured, the choices you make consistently and the environment you inhabit.

Below are five science-backed habits that researchers now believe are among the most powerful contributors to lasting well-being, not the fleeting kind, but the kind that compounds over time.

Habit 1: Invest in Your Relationships Like Your Life Depends on It (Because It Does)

The Harvard Study of Adult Development, one of the longest-running studies on adult life ever conducted, has tracked participants for over 80 years. Its conclusion, published and elaborated upon repeatedly in recent years, is striking: relationship quality predicts happiness, physical health, cognitive resilience and longevity — outperforming wealth, career success and even IQ as predictors of a good life.

Researchers now speak of social fitness as a core health behavior, comparable to exercise or sleep in that it requires regular, deliberate investment to maintain. A renowned 2015 meta-analysis found that social isolation carries health risks comparable to smoking 15 cigarettes a day. Recent biological research has linked loneliness to systemic inflammation and disease pathways.

We are not just emotionally dependent on connection; we are physiologically wired for it. This is why you need to treat relationship maintenance as non-negotiable. Whether you schedule it or simply show up. The returns, research suggests, are irreplaceable.

Habit 2: Protect Your Time More Fiercely Than Your Money

One of the most important insights from behavioral science in recent years is that this feeling of “time poverty” is one of the most corrosive forces acting on well-being.

Researcher Ashley Whillans of Harvard Business School has extensively documented this phenomenon. In her research, people who report feeling chronically time-poor (overwhelmed, rushed, without control over their daily hours) consistently score lower on measures of life satisfaction, positive affect, and mental health.

Conversely, using money to buy back time (outsourcing chores, paying for convenience, simplifying obligations, among others) is associated with greater well-being than spending the same money on material goods. Further research confirms this. A key 2017 study published in PNAS found that people who prioritized buying time over buying things reported significantly higher life satisfaction, yet relatively few people actually made this trade-off, suggesting a systematic miscalculation in how we allocate resources.

Before your next major financial or career decision, ask not just “what does this pay?” but “what does this cost me in time and autonomy?” Time affluence, or the felt sense that you have enough time and can direct how you spend it, is a well-being resource that money cannot directly buy but can sometimes purchase back.

Habit 3: Seek Experiences That Challenge (and Not Just Comfort) You

The standard model of a good life emphasizes happiness and meaning. But groundbreaking 2022 research published in Psychological Review introduced a third dimension that changes the picture considerably: psychological richness.

A psychologically rich life is not necessarily easy or pleasant. It is characterized by novelty, complexity, growth, and perspective-changing experiences. Experiences like travel, creative challenges, difficult learning and voluntary discomfort don’t always maximize immediate comfort, but they produce a life that, in retrospect, feels deep, varied and worth having lived.

In cross-cultural research spanning multiple countries, the researchers found that a meaningful portion of people, when asked what kind of life they’d want to have lived, chose the psychologically rich life over the happy or meaningful one, suggesting it represents a genuinely distinct human aspiration. People who perpetually optimize for comfort often find, years later, that their memories are thin and interchangeable. People who accept challenge, difficulty, and novelty accumulate a richer interior archive.

To exercise this habit, build in one experience per month that stretches you. It could be something unfamiliar, demanding, or perspective-altering. The short-term discomfort is often the price of a life that feels, when looking back, richly lived.

Habit 4: Spend on Others, Not Just on Yourself

In a 2023 systematic review, examining data across dozens of studies and multiple cultures, researchers concluded that spending on others reliably produces positive effects on subjective well-being. The effect held across income levels, cultures, and types of giving, whether direct donation, buying something for a friend, or volunteering time.

The authors argue that human psychology evolved in a context of deep interdependence. Contributing to others activates reward systems, reinforces social bonds and generates a sense of agency and significance that passive consumption cannot replicate. In short, we are not wired to be merely recipients. We are wired to give.

Take this as a sign to build some form of regular giving into your life: financial, temporal, or relational. Even small acts of prosocial behavior, practiced consistently, accumulate into a meaningful uplift in well-being.

Habit 5: Spend 120 Minutes a Week in Nature (No Exceptions)

In a landmark 2019 study published in Scientific Reports, researchers analyzed data from nearly 20,000 people and found that those who spent at least 120 minutes per week in natural environments reported significantly better health and psychological well-being than those who spent no time in nature.

Crucially, the effect emerged at the 120-minute threshold: less time showed weaker results, and the hours could be accumulated across the week in smaller doses rather than requiring a single long outing.

The mechanisms appear to involve reduced physiological stress responses, decreased rumination, and restoration of directed attention that daily cognitive demands deplete. Increasingly, researchers view exposure to nature not as recreation but as a basic input into human functioning. This means that exposure to nature is something our nervous system appears to require in ways that urban environments don’t provide.

What makes this finding especially important is its accessibility. Unlike most well-being interventions, regular time in nature is largely free, requires no expertise, and works across cultures and demographic groups.

The final habit is to treat 120 minutes of nature per week as a non-negotiable health behavior, equivalent to sleep or exercise. Break it into 20-minute daily walks if needed. The threshold is clear. The benefits are real.
